concepts.definition: A starter or dough is ready when observable evidence (rise, bubble structure, aroma, surface dome) matches the intended stage. Elapsed time is only a prediction that temperature can change.
Hydration is the weight of water divided by the weight of flour, expressed as a percentage. Higher hydration makes a slacker dough that needs more strength-building to hold its shape.

scenarios.title: Rescue a sluggish starter
scenarios.context: A fictional baker's starter has barely risen six hours after feeding in a cool kitchen. No real kitchen is involved.
scenarios.task: Decide what to do next and explain the evidence you would wait for.
requirements: State the decision and the evidence behind it.
Name one alternative and how you would compare the results.
scenarios.model: Keep the starter somewhere a little warmer and check it every hour. Mix only when it has roughly doubled, shows bubbles through its depth and a domed top. Record the temperature so the next prediction improves.
scenarios.reasoning: A strong response ties each choice to evidence the baker can observe, keeps an alternative open and says what result would change the plan.

scenarios.title: Choose a hydration for a first loaf
scenarios.context: A fictional beginner wants an open crumb but struggles to shape slack doughs. No real bakery is involved.
scenarios.task: Recommend a hydration and a folding plan, and say how you would move toward a wetter dough later.
requirements: State the decision and the evidence behind it.
Name one alternative and how you would compare the results.
scenarios.model: Start near 70% hydration with three sets of folds, then raise the water in small steps as shaping becomes reliable. Compare crumb and shape between steps rather than jumping straight to a very wet dough.
scenarios.reasoning: A strong response ties each choice to evidence the baker can observe, keeps an alternative open and says what result would change the plan.

scenarios.title: Plan a weekend bake for the Larkfield café
scenarios.context: The fictional Larkfield café wants country loaves on Saturday and Sunday mornings from one home oven. Use the [hydration lab](#/course/hearth/labs/hearth-lab-hydration) to check the recipe, the [fermentation lesson](#/lesson/hearth-m01-l01) to plan the starter, and the [oven module](#/module/hearth-m03) for the bake itself. The [bake-plan guide](#/course/hearth/guides/hearth-guide-bake-plan) gives a template, and the [starter scenario](#/practice/hearth-m01-scenario) is a smaller warm-up. The [course map](#/course/hearth) lists everything else.
scenarios.task: Write a two-day bake plan with the checks that end each wait and a fallback if the dough runs late.
requirements: State the decision and the evidence behind it.
Name one alternative and how you would compare the results.
scenarios.model: Feed the starter on Friday evening, mix when it peaks, bulk ferment by evidence and shape into a cold proof overnight. Bake from the fridge in batches, uncovering each pot after 20 minutes. If the dough runs late, extend the cold proof rather than baking an under-proofed loaf. The [village bakery case](#/course/hearth/cases/hearth-case-village-bakery) shows the same cold-proof idea at a larger scale.
scenarios.reasoning: A strong response ties each choice to evidence the baker can observe, keeps an alternative open and says what result would change the plan.

scenarios.title: Scale the bake for a market stall
scenarios.context: A fictional baker wants to double production for a Saturday market without buying a second oven. No real market is involved.
scenarios.task: Propose a schedule that fits twice the loaves through one oven and say what you would measure on the first market day.
requirements: State the decision and the evidence behind it.
Name one alternative and how you would compare the results.
scenarios.model: Stagger two doughs by ninety minutes so each is ready when the oven is free, and keep both on cold proofs so a delay costs little. Measure bake times, oven recovery between batches and how many loaves sold per hour to plan the next market.
scenarios.reasoning: A strong response ties each choice to evidence the baker can observe, keeps an alternative open and says what result would change the plan.

labs.title: Calculate hydration from a recipe
labs.summary: Run a small script that converts a recipe into its true hydration, counting the starter.
labs.outcome: Explain a dough's hydration from its weights and predict how it will handle.
labs.environment: Python 3.12 standard library; no network access or extra packages.
labs.evidence: Synthetic fixture: the expected output was written by hand for this test and no execution is claimed.

labs.title: Plan a bake schedule on paper
labs.summary: Lay out a two-day timeline from starter feeding to cooling and find the step that constrains the rest.
labs.outcome: Build a timeline that names its waiting points and the evidence that ends each wait.
labs.environment: Pen and paper or a text editor.
labs.evidence: Your written timeline, compared with the worked schedule in the lab text.
